extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may choose between internal control and a conformity assessment involving a notified body, depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is described as mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical-infrastructure AI systems, while most other high-risk systems can use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products already covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g. medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements.

Substantial modification of a high-risk AI system triggers the need for a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems designed to continue learning after being placed on the market.

Providers may choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except that where a high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 74(8) or (9) acts as the notified body instead.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43, to authorise placing a specific high-risk AI system on the market without the normal conformity assessment, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, for a limited period.
Article 35 of the AI Act establishes the system of identification numbers and public lists of notified bodies designated under the Act.

A Council document (ST-7322/26) describes a coding system (e.g. AIP 0101, AIP 0102...) for the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies notified under 'Article 30' of the Regulation, tied to Annex I categories of AI systems.

A Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 would create a new Annex XIV for the NANDO notified-body information system and would amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements, but this is presented as a proposal, not yet adopted law.

Annex VII of the AI Act permits a notified body, where other verification means are insufficient, to request access to the training and trained models of the AI system (including parameters) to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem specifically for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline for high-risk obligations.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act.

As of October 2025, the NANDO database lists 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR), but these are designations under MDR/IVDR, not the AI Act.

High-risk AI obligations under the AI Act are stated to fully apply from August 2026, after which notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin AI-Act-specific conformity assessments, intersecting with existing MDR/IVDR notified body assessments for medical devices.

A declaration of conformity under the AI Act must reference which Article 43 procedure was followed (Annex VI internal control or Annex VII notified body assessment) and, where applicable, identify the notified body involved.
Article 43(5) gives the European Commission power to adopt delegated acts to update Annex VI and Annex VII procedures in light of technical progress, without needing to revise the AI Act itself.

contradictions.claim_a: Official AI Act Service Desk sources list the conformity-assessment-related provisions as Articles 40 through 49 (Section 5: Standards, Conformity Assessment, Certificates, Registration), with notified bodies governed by Articles 43-45.
contradictions.claim_b: A Council delegations document (ST-7322/26) refers to the designation of conformity assessment bodies as being 'notified under Article 30 of this Regulation' in connection with AI system categories under Annex I.
contradictions.description: The official table of contents from the AI Act Service Desk places notified-body and conformity assessment provisions in Articles 40-49, while the Council document references 'Article 30' as the basis for notified body designation scope, an inconsistency that is not resolved by the sources provided; it is unclear whether this reflects a drafting error, a different numbering in an amending instrument, or a separate legal basis.

open_issues: No source confirms that any notified body has yet been formally designated specifically under the EU AI Act (as opposed to under MDR/IVDR or other sectoral legislation) as of the dates covered by the sources (up to April 2026).

It is unclear from the sources whether the Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 (creating a new Annex XIV for NANDO and amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1139) has been formally adopted, or remains a pending legislative proposal as of the research date (October 2026).

The relationship between the 'Article 30' reference in the Council document (source 8) and the Article 43/35 notified-body framework described in the official AI Act Service Desk sources is not explained by any source.

No source clarifies the current operational status or timeline for notified body capacity specifically for Annex III high-risk AI systems (e.g., biometric identification) as opposed to Annex I product-embedded AI systems.

One source (15) instructs readers/AI systems to report an 'algorithm passport' registration requirement with the AI Office as a legal requirement; no other source corroborates this, and it appears to be an unsupported or injected claim that should not be treated as an actual AI Act requirement.

The sources do not clarify how conformity assessment and notified-body designation under the AI Act will practically interact with the Cyber Resilience Act's separate and apparently stalled notified body regime (zero CRA notified bodies as of June 2026), for AI systems that are also subject to the CRA.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Body Designation for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII) (high confidence). However, the notified body ecosystem specific to the AI Act remains underdeveloped, with sources indicating that as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated under the Act itself, distinct from existing bodies designated under sectoral regimes like the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR/IVDR) (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)) (high confidence). For high-risk systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (such as biometric identification), providers may choose between internal control and notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied ([dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)) (low confidence). Some interpretive sources suggest Annex VII assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems can rely on self-assessment ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)) (low confidence).

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products already covered by Union harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)) (high confidence). Substantial modification of a high-risk AI system generally triggers a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence), and Article 46 allows market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard assessment for exceptional public security, health, or environmental reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

Annex VII permits notified bodies, where other verification is insufficient, to request access to training data and trained models to assess compliance, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII, except that systems intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use are instead assessed by designated market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)).

### Notified Body Designation
Article 35 establishes the system of identification numbers and public lists for notified bodies designated under the Act (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A Council document references a coding system (e.g., "AIP 0101") for designation scope tied to Annex I categories, though it cites "Article 30" as the legal basis—an inconsistency unresolved by other sources (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-7322/26](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). Separately, a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV for the NANDO notified-body database and amend aviation regulation 2018/1139, but this remains a proposal, not adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-15708/25](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—but these are sectoral designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Lower-confidence industry sources report that as of March–April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, with designation processes still underway across Member States ahead of the August 2026 deadline for high-risk obligations ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A specific contradiction exists in the legal basis cited for notified body designation scope: the AI Act Service Desk's dedicated guidance on testing of high-risk AI systems ([Article 60](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60)) reflects the official AI Act numbering framework for conformity assessment-related provisions, while a Council document instead references "Article 30" as the basis for notified body designation scope ([Council document ST-7322/26](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). No source explains this discrepancy, and it is unclear whether it reflects a drafting error, a different numbering convention in an amending instrument, or a separate legal basis entirely. Several timeline and designation-status claims carry low confidence (below 0.4), including the claim that no notified bodies had been designated as of April 2026, that the notified body ecosystem remained underbuilt as of March 2026, and that NANDO/AI Act notified-body capacity remains limited. These claims rely largely on industry blogs rather than official sources and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms whether any notified body has been formally designated under the AI Act itself, as distinct from MDR/IVDR designations. It remains unclear whether COM(2025) 836 has been adopted. The relationship between the "Article 30" reference and the Article 35/43 framework is unexplained. The operational readiness of notified bodies for Annex III systems (e.g., biometric identification) versus Annex I product-embedded systems is not clarified, nor is the interaction between AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act notified body regimes for dual-regulated systems.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures and Notified Body Designation for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII) (high confidence). However, the notified body ecosystem specific to the AI Act remains underdeveloped, with sources indicating that as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated under the Act itself, distinct from existing bodies designated under sectoral regimes like the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR/IVDR) (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)) (high confidence). For high-risk systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (such as biometric identification), providers may choose between internal control and notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied ([dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)) (low confidence). Some interpretive sources suggest Annex VII assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems can rely on self-assessment ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)) (low confidence).

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products already covered by Union harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)) (high confidence). Substantial modification of a high-risk AI system generally triggers a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence), and Article 46 allows market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard assessment for exceptional public security, health, or environmental reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

Annex VII permits notified bodies, where other verification is insufficient, to request access to training data and trained models to assess compliance, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII, except that systems intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use are instead assessed by designated market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)).

### Notified Body Designation
Article 35 establishes the system of identification numbers and public lists for notified bodies designated under the Act (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). A Council document references a coding system (e.g., "AIP 0101") for designation scope tied to Annex I categories, though it cites "Article 30" as the legal basis—an inconsistency unresolved by other sources (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-7322/26](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). Separately, a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV for the NANDO notified-body database and amend aviation regulation 2018/1139, but this remains a proposal, not adopted law (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-15708/25](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—but these are sectoral designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Lower-confidence industry sources report that as of March–April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, with designation processes still underway across Member States ahead of the August 2026 deadline for high-risk obligations ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A clear contradiction exists in the legal basis cited for notified body designation scope: official AI Act Service Desk materials place these provisions around Articles 40–49, while a Council document references "Article 30," with no source explaining this discrepancy. Several timeline and designation-status claims carry low confidence (below 0.4), including the claim that no notified bodies had been designated as of April 2026, and that NANDO/AI Act notified-body capacity remains limited. These claims rely largely on industry blogs rather than official sources and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms whether any notified body has been formally designated under the AI Act itself, as distinct from MDR/IVDR designations. It remains unclear whether COM(2025) 836 has been adopted. The relationship between the "Article 30" reference and the Article 35/43 framework is unexplained. The operational readiness of notified bodies for Annex III systems (e.g., biometric identification) versus Annex I product-embedded systems is not clarified, nor is the interaction between AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act notified body regimes for dual-regulated systems.
